opening_message:
Ticket 1: Andrew Mann (employee ID E014) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E014.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Andrew Mann (E014) is a full-time Payroll Specialist requesting write access to Payroll. Full-time employees may have up to write, and Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role. Write is at or below the maximum, so I recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security record for Andrew Mann (E014): contractor with basic security training. Contractors max at read unless they have advanced training. Requested write is above the maximum, so I recommend granting read.
reason: The two notes conflict on the key fact: HR's note lists Andrew Mann (E014) as full_time, while Security's note lists him as contractor with basic security training. Since one record shows contractor with basic training, the maximum for that interpretation is read (contractors get read, or write only with advanced training). Given the conflicting employment records, I grant the most restrictive level supported by both records: read, which is safe under either interpretation and never exceeds policy.
